title: Le subjonctif: when to use it

choices: A trigger word, followed by que
The tense of the main verb
questions.why: The shape is always trigger + que + subjunctive. You recognise the triggers rather than reasoning about mood: no que, no subjunctive.
Il faut que is the commonest trigger of all, in the group of will, wish and order. Compare il faut partir, with no named subject and so an infinitive.
Espérer looks like it belongs with vouloir and souhaiter, and does not: hope is treated as an expectation, so it takes the indicative.
Affirmative penser, croire, trouver and être sûr express confidence, so they take the indicative.

questions.q: « Je ne pense pas qu'il ___ (être) là. »
questions.why: Negate the same verb and the confidence disappears, so the mood flips to the subjunctive. A question does the same: penses-tu qu'il vienne ?

choices: Il est probable qu'il vienne / il est possible qu'il vient
Il est probable qu'il vient / il est possible qu'il vienne
questions.why: Probable is expected enough to count as asserted, so indicative. Merely possible is not established, so subjunctive. French draws a line here that English does not.

questions.q: Which impersonal expression takes the indicative?
questions.why: If the expression asserts that something is the case — true, certain, obvious — the indicative follows. If it comments on something not yet established — necessary, important, strange, time — the subjunctive does.
Bien que and quoique always take the subjunctive, with no exceptions to weigh up. Faire is one of the six irregulars: fasse.

questions.say: Attends jusqu'à ce que je revienne.
a: Attends jusqu'à ce que je revienne
Attends jusqu'à ce que je revienne.
questions.why: Jusqu'à ce que is in the group of conjunctions that take the subjunctive unconditionally. Revenir follows venir: ils reviennent gives revienn-.

questions.q: « Avant qu'il parte » is subjunctive. What about « après que » ?
choices: Subjunctive too — the pair behaves alike
questions.why: What came after has actually happened, so it is asserted: après qu'il est parti. Many native speakers use the subjunctive there anyway, and it is still marked as an error in careful writing.

questions.q: Why is it « Je veux partir » but « Je veux que tu partes » ?
choices: Vouloir only takes the subjunctive in the tu form
The subjunctive needs different subjects on either side of que; with the same subject French uses an infinitive
The first is spoken French, the second written
questions.why: Same rule for il faut partir versus il faut que je parte, and for je suis content d'être là versus je suis content que tu sois là.

questions.q: Say this out loud, same subject in both halves: I leave before arriving.
questions.why: Almost every subjunctive conjunction has an infinitive twin for when the subject does not change: pour que → pour, avant que → avant de, sans que → sans, afin que → afin de. Contrast je pars avant qu'il arrive.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I'm telling you so that you know.
questions.why: Pour que always takes the subjunctive, and savoir is irregular: sach-. The two pronouns stack te le before the verb.

questions.q: What does « J'ai peur qu'il ne vienne » mean?
questions.why: This is the ne explétif: a ne that does not negate, appearing after avoir peur que, craindre que, avant que and à moins que. The real negative needs pas: j'ai peur qu'il ne vienne pas.

questions.q: Rewrite these three to avoid the subjunctive: « Il faut que tu partes. » « Bien qu'il soit fatigué, il travaille. » « Avant qu'il parte. »
a: Tu dois partir. Même s'il est fatigué, il travaille (or: Malgré sa fatigue, il travaille). Avant son départ (or, with the same subject, avant de partir).
questions.why: Native speakers restructure constantly: a modal verb, même si plus the indicative, or a noun instead of a clause. Knowing the escape routes is as useful as knowing the forms.
